meta.title: agentwatchdog — host-side runtime audit for AI coding agents
meta.description: Watches Claude Code, Codex CLI, aider and others from outside the agent — from /proc, where cooperation isn’t a variable. No hooks, no wrappers, no opt-out. Never reads your prompts.

hero.h1: Nothing on this host gets to decide whether it’s audited.
hero.lead: agentwatchdog watches AI coding agents from outside the agent — from `/proc`, where cooperation isn’t a variable. It never reads your prompts, and there is a test that fails if it ever does.

scan.title: Scan · 4 processes
scan.caption: Synthetic command lines, real rules. In the tool itself the raw string is never written at all — redaction happens before anything reaches disk, so there is no “before” on your host to reconstruct.

sections.h2: The tooling you already have needs the agent’s cooperation.
sections.intro: In-agent observability — OTel exporters, hooks, wrapper commands, proxies — works only while the agent plays along. Skip the environment variable, don’t install the hook, call the binary directly, and it goes blind. The runaway cron job, the misconfigured unit and the account that shouldn’t be here are precisely the cases that never play along.

rows.label: Can be bypassed
rows.us: **No.** A process that exists is seen

rows.label: Dependencies
rows.us: None. Python 3 standard library and systemd

rows.label: Prompt content
rows.us: Never read; redacted before anything is written

rows.label: Answers
rows.us: Who ran what, spawned by whom, behaving how

sections.note: Both are worth having. If you want per-token cost dashboards, use an OTel-based tool — this is not that. This is the audit trail for the machine.

sections.h2: Six things worth waking up for.
sections.intro: Every alert carries the command to run next. Repeats are suppressed per situation rather than per scan — one account running fifty agents is one finding, because a monitor that fires every sixty seconds is a monitor somebody turns off.

rows.body: An account outside `ALLOWED_USERS` ran an agent. The alert carries `loginuid`, so “alice ran an agent as root via sudo” arrives as a fact instead of a mystery.

One parent process keeps spawning agents. No human does this — it is a restart loop, and it bills you for every attempt. The alert carries the ancestry, because the agent is the symptom and the parent is the bug.
One account is starting agents faster than a person types.

A non-interactive agent outlived its limit. Interactive and SDK sessions are exempt: a session someone is sitting in front of is not a hung process, and treating it as one makes this useless on exactly the hosts it is for.
Sustained abnormal resource use. Measured as a lifetime average with a minimum sample age, so the spike every agent produces while starting up doesn’t become an alert every agent produces.
Several agents landing on a host that is already struggling. No single process is at fault, which is exactly why nothing else reports it.

sections.h2: Five promises, each with a test that fails if it breaks.
sections.intro: This thing reads command lines for a living. That is only acceptable if the limits are enforced rather than described — so every one below is wired to a test, and CI runs them as their own job, where a failure is impossible to miss.

rows.body: `/proc/PID/environ` is not opened on any code path. The test records every `open()` during a scan and fails if that file appears. API keys living in the environment cannot pass through this tool.
Command lines are redacted before they are written, using per-agent rules — because every CLI keeps its prompt somewhere different.

rows.h3: Positional arguments are denied by default.
rows.body: An argument survives only if a fingerprint vouches for it as a known subcommand. An unrecognised flag is treated as boolean, so the token after it is covered too. An agent released after this version leaks nothing; it only shows up with less detail.

rows.h3: Credential shapes are masked wherever they appear.
rows.body: Provider key prefixes, JWTs and long opaque tokens are masked even in positions no rule anticipated — which is where a credential ends up when somebody pastes a command wrong.

rows.h3: What may leave the host is anonymous by construction.
rows.body: The summary is assembled from scratch into a fixed shape rather than filtered out of an event, then checked against a key allowlist at runtime. An export that cannot be proven anonymous is refused, not published.

sections.note: Run `agentwatchdog selftest` to watch these hold against the agents actually running on your machine, not against ours.

sections.intro: Each agent is a JSON fingerprint describing how to recognise it and where it carries its prompt. Operators can add or correct one in `/etc/agentwatchdog/agents.d` without waiting for a release, and a fingerprint plus one redaction test is the easiest useful pull request this project takes.

rows.prompt: Positional, at top level and after `exec`

sections.note: Two traps the verified tables caught, as a caution against writing these from memory. Codex takes a prompt as a positional at the top level, not only after `exec`. And Codex’s `-p` is `--profile`, while Claude Code’s `-p` is the prompt — port one agent’s rules to the other and the tool dutifully masks a profile name while writing the prompt to disk. Both are now regression tests.

sections.intro: One file, nothing to build, no dependency beyond `python3`. Linux only — the design is `/proc`.

notes: Apache-2.0. An independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or any other agent vendor; product names identify the software being observed.

It observes and reports — it is not a sandbox and not a containment boundary. Intended for hosts you own or are authorised to audit, and deliberately unsuitable for surveilling people: no prompts, no keystrokes, no file contents.
